title: Fish Can't Climb Trees, But New York Students Can Learn Math
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman criticises New York's decision to drop passing the statewide Regents exams as a graduation requirement beginning with the class of 2028, replacing a common standard with locally designed assessment strategies. He seizes on a Regents board member's justification, the familiar cartoon line that you do not judge a fish by its ability to climb a tree, and argues it gets the issue almost exactly backward. Core academic subjects are not innate talents some children lack, he contends, and society has decided every child should learn them. The essay's central move is to reframe common assessments as a protection for different students rather than an injustice to them: without an external benchmark, adults can quietly lower expectations and award diplomas without anyone outside the school checking whether students can read, write or do math. Aldeman concedes fair questions about whether the Regents test the right material or set the right cut scores, and offers a middle path used by Georgia, North Carolina, South Carolina and Virginia, where end-of-course exams count toward course grades. New York's choice, he concludes, will make diplomas easier to earn and harder to interpret. (Close call between Practice & Culture and Learning & Curriculum; filed as Practice & Culture as a school-policy commentary, matching prior Aldeman policy pieces.)
points: Aldeman argues the fish-and-tree analogy implies some students could never meet common standards, which he treats as a form of lowered expectations.
Common assessments matter precisely because students differ, since they stop schools from quietly lowering the bar for struggling students.
New York will still administer high school tests under federal requirements, but from 2028 performance on them will carry no graduation consequence, decoupling the diploma from an external standard.
He proposes a compromise used in several Southern states and under consideration in Massachusetts: end-of-course exams counted as a portion of course grades rather than a strict gateway.
The net effect, he concludes, is diplomas that are easier to earn but whose meaning is harder to know.
quotes: Except, think about what Thomas-Williams is saying here. She’s arguing that it’s not fair to have one common benchmark in English Language Arts, math, science, and social studies. She’s implying that it’s unfair to certain students to hold them to the same standards, because of course they could never be able to meet them.

Fundamentally, the fish-and-tree analogy gets the issue almost exactly backward. English, math, science, and social studies are not innate talents that some children possess and others do not, like a fish not being able to climb trees.
In fact, common assessments matter because students are different. Without them, it becomes much easier for adults to quietly lower expectations for students who are struggling.

A common benchmark says that regardless of which school you attend, how much money your family makes, or what your teachers expect of you, the state believes you are capable of learning the same core academic content as everyone else.

But beginning with students graduating in 2028, students will no longer have to demonstrate any particular level of performance on those exams. Instead, districts and schools will make up their own rules.
Under this model, teachers control most of a student’s grade, but a common state assessment provides an external measure of whether the student learned the material.

Instead, New York is taking the common benchmark out of the diploma itself. That will make it easier for more students to earn a diploma. But it will also make it harder to know what that diploma means.
